posts.title: Everyone Is Talking About AI. But Are Businesses Actually Getting Value From It?
posts.body:
Everyone is talking about AI, and companies are pouring real money into it. The harder question is whether that money is actually producing results.

Research the Wall Street Journal highlighted recently points to a familiar problem: AI budgets keep growing, but plenty of leaders still can't clearly say what return they're getting for that spend. Honestly, that shouldn't surprise anyone. It's easy for a company to decide "we need AI." It's much harder to answer the follow-up question — what exactly are we going to use it for, and how will we know it worked?

AI shouldn't be adopted just because everyone else seems to be doing it. A business should start with the problem it's trying to solve, not the tool. Maybe that's automating repetitive admin work. Maybe it's improving customer support response times. Maybe it's helping the IT team catch security threats earlier. Maybe it's making sense of data that's been sitting unused for years. Whatever it is, the technology should follow the business problem, not the other way around.

Governance is the other piece companies tend to skip. Who's actually allowed to use AI tools at your company? What information are employees allowed to put into them? Which tools are approved, and who's keeping an eye on how they're used? What's the plan if an AI system gets something wrong? These used to feel like theoretical questions. They aren't anymore — AI has moved out of the experimentation phase and into everyday operations for a lot of businesses, including ones that never had a real policy conversation about it.

If there's one lesson I keep coming back to, it's this: don't measure your AI strategy by how many AI tools your company has adopted. Measure it by the problems those tools have actually solved. The companies that get that right tend to get far more value out of AI than the ones just chasing whatever's trending.

posts.title: AI Is Changing Cybersecurity — and the Game Is Getting Faster
posts.excerpt: AI Is Changing Cybersecurity — and the Game Is Getting Faster
posts.body:
AI has completely changed how we talk about cybersecurity, and it happened faster than most of us expected.

For years, the conversation was mostly one-sided: AI as a tool for defenders. It helps security teams sift through enormous volumes of data, spot anomalies, and catch threats that would take a human analyst far longer to find. That story is still true. But it's no longer the whole story.

AI is also getting very good at finding weaknesses in software and systems — and not just in the hands of security researchers. Recent research and a growing number of real-world incidents show how quickly that capability is maturing on the offensive side too. The same tool that helps a security team find a vulnerability before criminals do can, in someone else's hands, help find that same vulnerability faster than ever.

That puts us in an odd position. Cybersecurity is turning into a race between AI-powered attacks and AI-powered defence, and I don't think that's a problem only for the Googles and Microsofts of the world. Banks, schools, hospitals, small and medium businesses, government offices, even a small office back room — all of them now run on cloud services, Windows machines, networks and web applications. The attack surface has gotten a lot bigger, and it keeps growing.

For IT professionals, that makes the fundamentals matter more, not less. Keep systems patched. Monitor your endpoints and your network. Keep user privileges tight. Protect your backups properly. Use strong authentication everywhere it counts. Know exactly what's running in your environment. And don't assume the controls that worked well last year will automatically hold up against an AI-driven threat landscape — that's worth checking, not assuming.

AI is making cybersecurity more powerful. It's also, unfortunately, making cyberattacks more powerful. The organizations that take that seriously now — rather than after an incident — will be in a much stronger position.

I think the future of cybersecurity isn't really humans fighting attackers anymore. Increasingly, it's machines fighting machines, with humans responsible for making sure their machines are pointed in the right direction.

#AI #Cybersecurity #InformationTechnology #IT #ArtificialIntelligence #Technology

posts.title: Windows 11 Is Getting More Security-Focused — and IT Administrators Should Pay Attention
posts.excerpt: Windows 11 Is Getting More Security-Focused — and IT Administrators Should Pay Attention
posts.body:
If you manage Windows machines for a living, there's something worth paying attention to in Windows 11 right now: security is becoming baked into the operating system itself, not just something antivirus software bolts on afterward.

One example is Microsoft's plan to roll out Memory Integrity to more eligible devices. It uses virtualization-based security to help shield critical parts of Windows from malicious or untrusted kernel-level code — the kind of low-level attack that's historically been hard to defend against. Microsoft is also continuing to tighten up Secure Boot and TPM reporting. And on the other side of the update, September 2026's Windows 11 release adds improvements to several AI components — Image Search, Content Extraction, Semantic Analysis — on supported Copilot+ PCs.

So Windows 11 is pushing in two directions at once: more AI capability, and more security underneath it.

For home users, most of this happens quietly in the background and doesn't require much thought. For IT administrators, it deserves a closer look. Managing business computers isn't just a question of whether Windows is running anymore — it's worth actually checking:

Are devices fully patched?
Is Secure Boot enabled?
Is TPM functioning the way it should?
Is Memory Integrity compatible with your applications and drivers, or will it break something?
Are security policies centrally managed, or left to whatever each machine happens to have?
Are users running with more admin privileges than they actually need?
Do you have working backups if something does go wrong?

Windows 11 is genuinely getting more security-conscious at the OS level, and that's a good thing. But an operating system can only do so much on its own — security still comes down to how the system is configured, managed and monitored day to day. For anyone responsible for Windows machines in a business setting, keeping up with changes like these is becoming just as important as keeping the machines running in the first place.
